name: Dead Signal // Interference Pattern Tee
description:
A band tee for Dead Signal, an industrial noise act out of the Shelf district that has been building a following in underground venues for two years. The shirt is black, printed on a heavy-weight synth-cotton that's already slightly stiff from the screen printing process. The front graphic is a dense, almost illegible interference pattern — overlapping waveforms that resolve into a face if you look at it from a specific angle in certain light. The back has a tour date list from their first corridor run, most of the dates for venues that no longer exist.

This specific design is from their 'Null/Null' run — a series of shows where they allegedly played the same set in reverse on alternating nights. Whether that's true or promotional mythology, no one is entirely sure. The shirts were sold at shows only, cash only, no receipts. Seeing one in the wild means something to people who were there.
what_it_says: You were there, or you know someone who was. Either way, you orbit something underground and real.
worn_by: people who trade on underground cultural capital
manufacturer: Dead Signal (self-produced, printed at a Shelf market stall)
story_hooks: One of the venues on the back of the shirt — listed as 'Sub/Null, Shelf Block 14' — was a front for something. The people who ran it disappeared after the run ended.

Dead Signal's lead vocalist has gone silent for six months. No statement, no posts, no sightings. People in the scene are starting to split between 'they're working on something' and 'something happened.'
A Tier 4 music licensing corponation has offered to sign Dead Signal to a 'heritage label' — a move the band's community considers a death sentence for what they actually are.

physical_description.visual_profile: A heavy, slightly rigid band tee with an avant-garde aesthetic. The front presents a deliberately cryptic interference pattern that shifts visually depending on viewing angle—dense, overlapping waveforms that coalesce into a human face under specific lighting. The graphic has the intentional obscurity of underground industrial culture. Worn by people who were present at specific underground moments.
physical_description.fit: Relaxed, slightly boxy cut typical of screen-printed band merchandise. The heavy synth-cotton blend gives it structural weight rather than drape. Sits slightly stiff on the body, particularly in the first few wears before the fabric softens.
physical_description.primary_material: Heavy-weight synth-cotton blend, screen-printed. The material has industrial durability with a slight sheen from synthetic fibers. The printing sits raised on the fabric surface.
physical_description.texture: Rough, slightly stiff texture from the screen-printed graphic. The ink creates tactile ridges across the front. The base fabric feels coarse, almost canvas-like—deliberately utilitarian rather than soft. Will soften gradually with wear.
physical_description.color_scheme: Solid black base with white/silver interference pattern graphic on front. The back tour dates printed in faded white or grey ink, deliberately degraded-looking as if already aged.
physical_description.closures: None—simple crew neck pullover, no buttons or zippers
distinctive_features: Angle-dependent holographic effect on front graphic—waveforms resolve into a face only at specific viewing angles
Back features printed tour dates from first corridor run, many referencing defunct venues
'Null/Null' run designation (implicit in graphic design philosophy)
Hand-made aesthetic despite screen printing—minor registration imperfections suggesting limited, artisanal production
Already shows wear pattern consistent with being worn repeatedly since initial sale
No official branding or UPC—pure underground artifact
physical_description.tier_indicator: Tier 4-5 subcultural currency. Not mass-produced or corporate. Value derives entirely from presence at specific underground events, not monetary cost.
physical_description.cultural_context: Marks the wearer as part of the Shelf district industrial/noise music underground. Signals attendance at dead-venue shows, participation in the 'Null/Null' mythology. Wearing one is a form of credibility within that scene—proof of presence at specific moments.
physical_description.condition_typical: Worn-in but cared for. Likely shows creasing from repeated wearing, slight fading on the graphic from body heat and friction. The original stiffness has softened. May show small fading or cracking on edges of printed graphic from washing and wear. Not trashed—this is a kept artifact, not disposable merchandise.
